note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: randomIndices has one entry per position, 0..2^31-1
clarifyingQuestions: May one ad fill several positions in a single call?
How is randomness supplied or seeded, and is a uniform choice required?
What is returned for a position with no eligible ad?
hints: An ad becomes ineligible either from its history or from being used earlier in this call.
Picking the r-th remaining eligible ad repeatedly is an order-statistic query on a shrinking list.
Keep a Fenwick tree of 1s over the eligible ads; descend it to find the (r+1)-th one, then clear it.
invariants: remaining equals the number of 1s in the Fenwick tree
eligible order is candidateAds order, fixed before assignment
chooseWhen: Many positions and many ads, where an O(P*A) refilter would be too slow
tradeoffs: Fenwick descent adds code over a plain list removal, which is O(A) per pick but simpler
hack2hire:6a19fed3c81f779dc6a2370d.variantLabel: Inferred variant 1: injected random index per position

clarifyingQuestions: Are times guaranteed strictly increasing?
Is an empty reading list possible?
hints: A period is a maximal run of consecutive qualifying readings.
Gaps between timestamps do not break a run; only a below-threshold reading does.
Scan once, remember the start time when a run opens, close it when the next reading fails or the array ends.
invariants: start is set exactly while inside a qualifying run
tradeoffs: None material; linear and constant extra space

constraints: each camera 0..1e5 readings, times strictly increasing
clarifyingQuestions: Is the second variant really an intersection of two cameras, and do they share one threshold?
Should touching periods [a,b] and [b,c] intersect at [b,b]?
hints: First reduce each camera to its sorted, disjoint motion periods.
Two sorted disjoint interval lists intersect like merging sorted lists.
Advance the pointer whose current period ends first; record [max start, min end] when it is nonempty.
invariants: periods of each camera are sorted and disjoint
every intersection pair is visited once
chooseWhen: Both inputs are sorted interval lists
tradeoffs: All-pairs checking is simpler but quadratic

clarifyingQuestions: Can a card type have zero cards?
Are only additions allowed (no removals)?
Is p bounded above?
hints: Each count must be raised to the next multiple of p; the cost for p is the sum of those gaps.
If q divides p, the next multiple of q is never farther than the next multiple of p, so only primes matter.
For a prime p, values in ((j-1)p, jp] all round to jp; prefix counts and sums give each block cost in O(1).
invariants: only primes up to max(2, max count) are candidates
zero counts cost nothing
chooseWhen: Large value range where per-element per-prime work is too slow
tradeoffs: Needs O(V) memory for prefix arrays

constraints: up to 5000 pages with outgoing links, 50000 links total
URLs are http:// with a lowercase host and optional path
clarifyingQuestions: How should concurrency be represented in a deterministic test?
Is the output order significant?
Does a port or https count as part of the hostname?
hints: Model the parser as a lookup table so the result does not depend on thread scheduling.
Only URLs on the start host are recorded or expanded.
Breadth-first search with a visited set; sort the visited set at the end.
invariants: every URL in the visited set has the start hostname
each URL is expanded at most once
chooseWhen: Any graph traversal over an injected adjacency map
tradeoffs: A real thread pool needs a shared visited set and termination detection; the deterministic model drops that
hack2hire:692f515ecd79766b0b310123.variantLabel: Deterministic model of the concurrent crawler

clarifyingQuestions: Is the task filtering one menu, or reconciling yesterday's and today's menus?
Should a category with no remaining active items be dropped?
What is returned when the root is inactive?
hints: An inactive node hides everything beneath it.
Copy only active children, preserving order.
Use an explicit stack of (source, copy) pairs so deep trees do not overflow recursion.
invariants: every copied node is active and has an active ancestor chain
the input tree is never modified
chooseWhen: Very deep trees where recursion is risky
tradeoffs: Recursive filtering is shorter but limited by recursion depth

clarifyingQuestions: Is water boundary measured in shared edges or in distinct water cells?
Do grid borders count as boundary?
In what order should islands be reported?
hints: Flood-fill each unvisited land cell to find its island.
While visiting a land cell, every in-grid neighbour that is water adds one boundary side.
Report [area, boundary] in the row-major order in which islands are first met.
invariants: each land cell is visited exactly once
each land-water side is counted once from its land cell
tradeoffs: Union-find works too but needs a second pass for aggregates

clarifyingQuestions: Is the count inclusive of the given index?
What should be returned: only count results or one entry per request?
hints: A flip of the whole string only toggles a global state.
Precompute prefix counts of ones in the original string.
With an odd number of flips, ones in [0,i] equal (i+1) minus the original count.
invariants: flipped parity equals the number of flips mod 2
prefix array is built once
tradeoffs: Range flips would need a segment tree instead

constraints: parentIndex forms a valid forest; roots are self-parents
clarifyingQuestions: How should deleted nodes be represented in the result?
Can a parent index be larger than the child index?
hints: Deleting a node removes exactly its descendants.
Build child lists from parent pointers.
Traverse from the deleted node with an explicit stack and mark each visited node -1.
invariants: deleted set is closed under descendants
surviving nodes keep their parent
chooseWhen: Single deletion on a parent-pointer forest
tradeoffs: Walking ancestors of every node avoids the child lists but is O(n * depth)

clarifyingQuestions: Are deletions applied in sequence on the same forest?
Is deleting an already deleted node an error or a no-op?
hints: Build child lists once and reuse them for every deletion.
Skip a deletion whose node is already gone.
During traversal never re-enter a deleted node, so total work stays linear.
invariants: each node is marked deleted at most once
tradeoffs: Requires O(n) adjacency memory up front

constraints: driver ids 0..1e9, added once before use
clarifyingQuestions: What units are rates and times in, and how should the total be rounded?
Can a delivery reference an unknown driver?
hints: Avoid floating point: keep rate in cents per hour and time in seconds.
Each delivery adds rate * seconds; the total in cents is that sum / 3600.
Round once at the end, half-up, using integer arithmetic.
invariants: total equals the sum over deliveries of rate * duration
chooseWhen: Money totals that must be exact
tradeoffs: Formatting as a string loses numeric convenience for callers

constraints: driver ids 0..1e9, added once before use
clarifyingQuestions: Does payUpTo pay deliveries by end time or by start time?
Are later-added deliveries that ended before a past payUpTo paid automatically?
hints: Keep a separate unpaid running sum.
Paying up to t removes every unpaid delivery whose end time is at most t.
A min-heap keyed by end time lets each delivery be paid exactly once.
invariants: unpaid sum equals the sum over deliveries still in the heap
chooseWhen: Repeated payouts over a growing ledger
tradeoffs: Heap adds O(log D) per insertion

constraints: driver ids 0..1e9, added once before use
clarifyingQuestions: Is "active" measured in drivers or in deliveries?
Are delivery intervals half-open?
Is the 24-hour window inclusive at both ends?
hints: Only deliveries overlapping [now-86400, now] matter; clip them to that window.
Merge each driver's clipped intervals so a driver counts once.
Sweep start (+1) and end (-1) events, ends first at equal times, and track the maximum.
invariants: each driver contributes at most 1 at any instant
max is attained at the window start or at some delivery start
chooseWhen: Peak concurrency queries over interval data
tradeoffs: Per-query cost is O(D log D); many queries over large ledgers are slow

clarifyingQuestions: Does a freeze override an allowed window?
What should malformed records do?
Is the answer a minute count or a list of windows?
hints: The week has only 10080 minutes, so per-minute coverage is affordable.
Use difference arrays for allowed and freeze coverage.
A minute counts when allowed coverage > 0 and freeze coverage == 0.
invariants: prefix sums give the exact coverage count of each minute
tradeoffs: Interval algebra would avoid the O(W) scan for huge domains

clarifyingQuestions: Should windows wrap from Sunday night into Monday morning?
Are adjacent deployable windows merged?
hints: Reuse the per-minute coverage from variant 1.
Scan minutes and open a window when a deployable run starts.
Close it at the first non-deployable minute or the week end.
invariants: emitted windows are maximal, disjoint and increasing
tradeoffs: No wrap-around merging is performed

constraints: account ids 1..8 lowercase letters or digits
clarifyingQuestions: What does transfer return on failure, and is a self-transfer allowed?
hints: A map from account id to balance is enough.
Validate existence and funds before changing anything.
Return the source balance after a successful transfer.
invariants: failed operations change no state
tradeoffs: No history is kept

constraints: account ids 1..8 lowercase letters or digits
clarifyingQuestions: What counts as outgoing?
How are ties ranked and how is each entry formatted?
hints: Track outgoing totals alongside balances.
Sort accounts by outgoing descending, then id ascending.
Format each as id(total) and take the first n.
invariants: outgoing only grows
chooseWhen: Rankings queried far less often than updates
tradeoffs: Sorting on each query costs O(A log A)

constraints: account ids 1..8 lowercase letters or digits
clarifyingQuestions: What is the cashback rate and delay?
At which moment does the cashback become visible?
Is the payment id global or per account?
hints: Payments behave like withdrawals that also schedule a cashback.
Because timestamps increase, scheduled cashbacks are already in due order: a FIFO queue works.
Before every operation, apply all cashbacks due at or before its timestamp.
invariants: cashback queue is ordered by due time
each cashback is applied exactly once
tradeoffs: A heap would be needed if due delays varied

constraints: account ids 1..8 lowercase letters or digits
clarifyingQuestions: What happens to the merged-away account's pending cashbacks and payment statuses?
Can a merged-away id be reused?
What should getBalance return for a time when the account did not exist?
hints: Merging moves balance, outgoing totals, payment ownership and pending cashbacks.
Record each account's balance after every change, with the time of the change.
Answer a historical balance with binary search over that account's change times; record an "absent" marker at merge time.
invariants: history times per id are nondecreasing
cashbacks are recorded at their due time, which precedes the operation that triggers them
tradeoffs: History grows with every change
hack2hire:687c5c0b024483ac76db8ca2.variantLabel: Inferred level 4: merge and historical balance

constraints: shuffledDeck is a permutation of the 52 [suit, rank] cards
clarifyingQuestions: Is dealing round-robin or in contiguous blocks?
How should shuffling be made testable?
Is the ace low or high in the sort order?
hints: Inject the shuffled deck instead of calling a random generator.
Deal card i to player i mod 4.
There are only 52 cards: mark each player's cards by canonical index and read them back in order.
invariants: each card goes to exactly one player
tradeoffs: Comparison sorting is equally fine at this size

constraints: shuffledDeck is a permutation of the 52 [suit, rank] cards
clarifyingQuestions: What happens to cards that cannot be dealt evenly?
hints: Each player gets floor(52 / players) cards.
Deal only the first players * floor(52 / players) cards round-robin.
Sort each hand by canonical index.
invariants: all hands have equal size
tradeoffs: Leftover cards are silently undealt

constraints: shuffledDeck is a permutation of the 52 [suit, rank] cards
clarifyingQuestions: What are the round rules, and how is card strength ordered?
Should the result be the winner or per-player round counts?
hints: If every player always plays their strongest remaining card, round r compares each player's r-th strongest card.
Encode strength as rank * 4 + suit.
Sort each hand descending once, then compare column by column.
invariants: cards are distinct, so every round has a unique winner
chooseWhen: Greedy play where order is fixed by sorting
tradeoffs: Rules are fully inferred

clarifyingQuestions: What does a placement return?
Should lines created for the opponent by the shift count?
Does play stop after a win?
hints: Bottom insertion shifts every piece in that column, so only lines through that column can change.
Store each column as a list appended at the bottom end.
For every height in the column, count runs of the mover in four directions, capped at k.
invariants: other columns are unchanged by a placement
tradeoffs: Checking every height costs O(h * k) per move

clarifyingQuestions: Does setting a property to its current value create an undo entry?
What does undo return when there is nothing to undo?
hints: Store, for each change, the value before and after.
Undo restores the before value, deleting the key if it was absent.
A stack gives the most recent change first.
invariants: state equals applying all changes left on the undo stack in order
tradeoffs: Memory grows with the number of changes

clarifyingQuestions: Does a new change discard the redo history?
hints: Undone changes move to a redo stack.
Redo re-applies the after value and moves the change back.
Any new change clears the redo stack.
invariants: undo stack + redo stack is the full linear history
tradeoffs: Branching histories are not kept

clarifyingQuestions: Is removing an absent key an undoable change?
How should listed properties be ordered?
hints: Treat removal as a change whose after value is "absent".
A failed removal records nothing.
List a layer's properties sorted by key.
invariants: absent is distinct from the empty string
tradeoffs: Listing sorts on each call

clarifyingQuestions: What exact strings represent scores?
What is the numeric view?
hints: Keep two point counters and a winner.
A game is won at 4+ points with a 2-point lead.
Map points to Love/15/30/40 unless both reach 3: then Deuce or Advantage.
invariants: no points change after a winner exists
tradeoffs: String formats are inferred

clarifyingQuestions: Does the follow-up extend to a set or a match?
Is a tiebreak played at 6-6?
hints: Reuse game scoring and count games.
A set ends at 6+ games with a 2-game lead.
At 6-6 switch to a tiebreak won at 7+ points with a 2-point lead.
invariants: points reset after each game
nothing changes after the set winner exists
tradeoffs: Rules are inferred from standard tennis

clarifyingQuestions: Is the size filter strict and in which direction?
Should results be names or full paths, and in what order?
hints: Store files in a directory trie.
Walk to the requested directory and collect every file below it.
Apply all filters (AND) and sort the matching paths.
invariants: find never visits files outside the directory subtree
tradeoffs: A flat path map is simpler when queries usually cover everything

clarifyingQuestions: Which combinators are needed for extensibility?
What do empty AND/OR mean?
hints: Treat filters as an expression tree.
Compile it once per query into a predicate.
Leaves stay the same as variant 1; AND/OR/NOT combine them.
invariants: empty AND is true, empty OR is false
tradeoffs: Closures add call overhead per file
